name: Early Chinese palaces & tombs
summary: From the rammed-earth platforms of the Shang to the vast palace compounds of Qin and Han, early Chinese builders worked in pounded earth and timber, setting halls on raised terraces along a north–south axis. Little survives above ground, so these buildings are known from excavated foundations, clay house models and above all from tombs, which were laid out as underground palaces for the dead.
image_file: Tomb of the First Emperor Qin Shi Huang Di, Xi'an, China - panoramio.jpg
image_caption: The tomb mound of the First Emperor near Xi'an

name: The Great Wall
summary: Walls of rammed earth, rubble and later brick and stone were built by rival states of the Warring States period, joined and extended by the Qin and Han, and rebuilt on a vast scale by the Ming. The Great Wall is not one structure but a system of walls, watchtowers, passes and garrisons stretched along the northern frontier over two thousand years.
image_file: The Great Wall of China at Jinshanling-edit.jpg
image_caption: The Ming Great Wall at Jinshanling, Hebei

name: Buddhist cave temples & early pagodas
summary: Buddhism reached China along the Silk Road, bringing the rock-cut sanctuary and the stupa. Chinese builders carved cave temples into cliffs at Dunhuang, Yungang and Longmen and transformed the Indian stupa into the many-storeyed pagoda, first in timber and then in brick and stone, which became one of the defining forms of East Asian architecture.

name: Tang & Liao timber halls
summary: The Tang dynasty perfected the Chinese timber frame: columns carrying clusters of interlocking brackets (dougong) that support deep, gently curving eaves. Only a handful of Tang halls survive, in remote mountain temples, but the Liao dynasty in the north continued the style, and the system spread to Korea and Japan, where Tang forms are preserved better than in China itself.

name: Asuka & Nara temple architecture
summary: Buddhism came to Japan from Baekje in the sixth century, and with it Korean and Chinese carpenters, roof-tile makers and painters. Temple compounds with a pagoda, a golden hall and cloisters were built at Asuka and then at Nara, the capital laid out on the Chinese grid. They include the oldest surviving wooden buildings in the world, at Hōryū-ji.
image_caption: Golden hall and pagoda of Hōryū-ji

name: Shinto shrine architecture
summary: Shinto shrines preserve forms older than Buddhist architecture in Japan: raised floors, thatched or bark roofs, unpainted timber and crossed finials. Ise and Izumo represent the two most ancient types, kept alive by periodic rebuilding rather than by preserving old fabric, while later shrines such as Itsukushima absorbed the colour and planning of Buddhist and palace architecture.

name: Three Kingdoms, Silla & Goryeo Buddhist architecture
summary: The Korean kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla adopted Buddhism in the fourth to sixth centuries and became the bridge that carried Chinese building to Japan. Their great timber temples are lost, but stone pagodas, the granite grotto of Seokguram and the terraces of Bulguksa show a distinctive refinement, and a few Goryeo timber halls are the oldest wooden buildings in Korea.
image_file: Lotus Flower Bridge and Seven Treasure Bridge at Bulguksa in Gyeongju, Korea.jpg
image_caption: Lotus Flower and Seven Treasures Bridges, Bulguksa

name: Heian Pure Land halls & shinden-zukuri
name_native: 平安浄土建築・寝殿造
summary: In Heian Japan the court aristocracy lived in shinden-zukuri mansions, pavilions linked by corridors around a pond garden. The same idea, applied to Pure Land Buddhism, produced Amida halls set over water to evoke the Western Paradise, most famously the Phoenix Hall of Byōdō-in. Construction became lighter, more Japanese and more closely bound to landscape.

name: Song architecture & the Yingzao Fashi
summary: Song dynasty architecture became more elaborate and more standardised. In 1103 the court published the Yingzao Fashi, a building manual that fixed a modular system of timber sizes, bracket sets and labour quotas. Surviving Song halls and pagodas show slenderer proportions, richer bracketing and the beginnings of the decorative intensity of later imperial architecture.
image_caption: Pagoda of Fogong Temple, Ying County

name: Kamakura Buddhist & Zen architecture
name_native: 鎌倉仏教・禅宗様建築
summary: After the civil wars of the 1180s Japanese builders turned again to China. The monk Chōgen rebuilt Tōdai-ji in the bold 'Great Buddha style' from southern China, and Zen monasteries introduced the 'Zen style' of Song China, with curved window heads, dense bracketing and stone-floored halls laid out in a strict axial plan.

name: Muromachi gardens & shoin
summary: Zen monks and the Ashikaga shōguns created the classic Japanese garden: the strolling pond garden, the dry landscape (karesansui) of raked gravel and stone, and the garden meant to be viewed from a veranda. Indoors, the shoin study with its alcove, staggered shelves and built-in desk became the model for the formal Japanese room.

name: Ming–Qing imperial architecture
summary: The Ming and Qing courts built on a scale never seen before: the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, imperial tombs and vast garden palaces, all governed by strict hierarchies of colour, roof form and number. Construction was run by official bureaus and hereditary families of designers such as the Lei. The Qing also patronised Tibetan Buddhist architecture, whose own great monument, the Potala in Lhasa, belongs to a separate tradition.
image_file: The Forbidden City - View from Coal Hill.jpg
image_caption: The Forbidden City seen from Jingshan (Coal Hill)

name: Chinese scholar gardens
summary: In the prosperous cities of the lower Yangzi, above all Suzhou, retired officials and merchants built walled gardens of rockeries, ponds, pavilions and covered walkways. Designed to unfold as a sequence of framed views, like a handscroll painting, they compress a whole landscape into a city plot. Ji Cheng's treatise Yuanye of 1631 set out their principles.

name: Momoyama & early Edo castles and palaces
summary: The wars of unification produced the Japanese castle: a many-storeyed keep (tenshu) of plastered timber on a high stone base, surrounded by moats and baileys. Their audience halls, painted with gold-ground screens, and the shrine-mausolea of the Tokugawa at Nikkō represent the most opulent phase of Japanese architecture.

name: Sukiya & the tea house
summary: Against Momoyama splendour, tea masters such as Sen no Rikyū developed the tiny rustic tea room of earth walls, bamboo and paper, entered through a low door. The sukiya style that grew from it, with natural materials, asymmetry and understated refinement, shaped villas such as Katsura and remains a living ideal of Japanese domestic architecture.

name: Joseon palaces & seowon
summary: The Joseon dynasty laid out its capital at Hanyang (Seoul) according to Confucian ritual and geomancy, with palaces set against mountains, the ancestral shrine of Jongmyo and city walls. Its architecture is restrained, with painted dancheong brackets, and closely fitted to terrain. In the countryside, Confucian academies (seowon) and gentry gardens expressed the scholarly ideals of Neo-Confucianism.
image_file: Front view of the Imperial Throne Hall Geunjeongjeon at Gyeongbokgung Palace with blue sky in Seoul.jpg

name: Vernacular houses & villages
summary: Beyond palaces and temples, farmers and clans built houses adapted to climate and community: the fortified earthen tulou of the Hakka in Fujian, the steep thatched gasshō farmhouses of the Japanese Alps and the tiled and thatched yangban villages of Korea. They are now among the most visited heritage sites of the region.
image_file: Three round, one oval, one square (16831811084).jpg
image_caption: Tianluokeng tulou cluster, Nanjing County, Fujian

name: Meiji Western-style & early modern
name_native: 明治洋風建築・近代建築
summary: After 1868 the Meiji government hired foreign architects such as Josiah Conder to teach Western building, and his Japanese students produced brick banks, stations and palaces in European styles. Frank Lloyd Wright and Antonin Raymond brought modern ideas, while in China architects trained abroad sought a modern national style, as in the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum.

name: Japanese modernism & Metabolism
name_native: モダニズム・メタボリズム
summary: Postwar reconstruction made Japan a centre of modern architecture. Kunio Maekawa and Kenzō Tange fused Le Corbusier's concrete with Japanese structural clarity, and in 1960 younger architects launched Metabolism, a vision of megastructures and replaceable capsules that would grow like organisms. In Korea Kim Swoo-geun and Kim Chung-up created a comparable modern architecture.

name: Contemporary architecture
summary: Since the 1980s East Asian architects have become leading figures worldwide, winning the Pritzker Prize repeatedly. Tadao Andō's concrete, Toyo Itō's and SANAA's lightness, Kengo Kuma's timber and Wang Shu's recycled tiles all reinterpret local tradition, while China's building boom has produced some of the largest projects on earth.
